gap: No result ChatGPT got states how little the advertised scan-rate gap is worth in time: summing each maker's own scan and report intervals, a 16K-scan board (Gamakay NS75) and a 128K-scan board (Epomaker HE75 V2) differ by 0.055 ms, about 1.3% of one frame at 240 Hz; nor that Yunzii's own page gives the 'Dual 8K' RT75 Pro 1 ms on wireless, which is eight 8,000 Hz report intervals.
standout_why: Compared against keebspicks.net (cited), Notebookcheck's HE75 Mag review (cited), dejaflow.com and setupinsider.com's under-$100 Hall effect page. Keebspicks and dejaflow list polling rates only, with no scan rates and no derived figures. Notebookcheck reports the HE75 Mag reached only 1,000 Hz wirelessly but computes nothing. Setupinsider (not cited, 60% boards) already converts 8,000 Hz to 0.125 ms against 1 ms at 1,000 Hz, and Epomaker's HE80 page does the same, so the report-interval conversion is not new. None adds the scan interval, puts the spread between boards against a frame, or sets Yunzii's 1 ms wireless figure against its 8K claim. The PC Gamer body did not load and computergear.co failed on a certificate error, so those two were not compared.
decides: It confirms rather than flips the pick. Among the three boards whose maker states both rates, the timing spread is 0.055 ms, so scan rate should not decide and price and connection should. On the prices read 2026-11-21, the Gamakay NS75 at $63.99 (tri-mode, 0.005 mm step) is $12.50 under the wired-figure leader Epomaker HE75 V2 at $76.49 (same 0.005 mm step), and $16.00 under the Yunzii RT75 Pro at $79.99. The RT75 Pro's wireless case is weaker than ChatGPT's 'best wireless gaming' label implies, because its maker states 1 ms wireless. This is incomplete: both AULA boards and the MCHOSE Jet 75 could not be opened, and no maker text I read gives the NS75's polling rate on 2.4 GHz.
